The plan is a simple row of rooms, the shape the costing counts: one outside door, a door in each cross wall, two windows to a room, walls 2.6 m high, eaves of 750 mm. Your build through the year

How the calendar is worked out

Soil tests take a week: the shrinkage box dries 7 days in shade (FAO). The trench, plinth, walls and plaster come from the quantities in Costing at CPWD output norms (InfraLens handbook): digging 1.5–2 m³ a labourer a day, rubble masonry 1–1.5 m³ a day, plaster 6–8 m² a day outside and 10–12 m² inside, for crews of one mason and two helpers working six days a week. The walls go at the pace set in Costing Low until you set your crew's. Blocks: CSEB at about 850 a day for seven people on an Auram 3000, cured four weeks before use (Auroville; ITDG); adobe moulded at 150 a person a day, our assumption Low, and dried 3–4 weeks before handling (NMSU). The walls dry 4–6 weeks for rammed earth (ERDEN); six weeks for cob and two for block walls are our estimates Low: check the walls, not the calendar. Lime plaster: 4–5 days between coats (Womersleys); limewash coats at least 12 hours apart and about three days of misting (Lime.org.uk); four coats of floor oil 1–2 days apart (Floors). Our estimates Low: setting out 2 days, the damp-proof course 1, the ring beam and roof 12, services and floor 7, and a week of floor drying.

Rainy months: for Hyderabad, the months above 50 mm in the Begumpet normals (Climate-Zone); for Chennai the northeast monsoon, October to December, Tamil Nadu's chief rainy season with 48 % of its rain; elsewhere the southwest monsoon, June to September, India's chief rainy season with about 75 % of the country's rain (IMD). Mark your own months if they differ. The red outline marks groundwork, walls or roof in a rainy month; plaster in the rains is shown in amber. A planning aid, not a programme; awaiting builder review.

Sources

Lifts of up to 600 mm and the "good hat and good pair of boots": East Dorset 2008; lifts of 40–80 cm, 61 cm on average, measured in 20 cob buildings of the Guérande peninsula: Poullain et al. 2024; 400–700 mm overhangs: New Forest National Park 2013; which way the walls face: Eco-Niwas Samhita 2018, Table 9 (see Sun and shade); ground falling away from the walls, and gravel footing drains: US National Park Service, Preservation Brief 5; rubble trench: Wikipedia (see Foundations); plinth, openings and lintels: IS 13827:1993 (see Structure); ground below the plinth: IHBC (see Repair and maintenance); damp-proof course: InfraLens, after IS 3067; drying: ERDEN 2023; topsoil: Auroville Earth Institute; limewash: Lime.org.uk. The order of the stages is ordinary practice; awaiting builder review.

Study

Soil lab: what is this earth good for?

Shake a sample with water in a jar and let it stand: sand drops within a minute, silt within about two hours, clay can take two days. Set the proportions, press Shake, and watch it settle.

Suitability, as dug

Ranges are a guide, not a rule: make test bricks or a test wall and leave them through a wet spell before you commit. A jar reads silt and clay lower than a laboratory does (FAO), so check it with the shrinkage box below.

Sources, and how sure

Particle sizes, and the ranges for rammed earth, pressed blocks and adobe: FAO, Farm Structures (tables 3.5 and 3.6, % by weight). Cob: 15–25 % clay to 75–85 % sand and silt, with about 2 % straw by weight, from the review by Haddad, Latif and Lannon 2023, which also finds no agreed mix. Plaster: 10–15 % clay and at least three parts sand to one of clay, from Practical Action. Light straw-clay: California Residential Code, Appendix BI; daub is grouped with it as a rich, sticky mix, a rule of thumb Low. The sand and silt bands set around those clay figures are this book's own Low. Ribbon lengths: Colorado State Extension (under 1 inch a loam, 1 to 2 inches a clay loam, over 2 a clay), tied to clay content by the class limits in TUM's soil texture flow chart (loam 7–27 % clay, clay loam 27–40 %, clay from 40 %); a real ribbon also depends on silt and water Low. Black cotton soil: Katti 1978, 50–70 % clay, mostly montmorillonite, about a third of India's surface deposits; the sample uses 50 %. Smectite clays such as montmorillonite can swell by up to 30 % (Purdue Extension); kaolinite shows no shrink–swell to speak of (Burras, Iowa State); FAO adds that soils with more than 30 % clay shrink and swell a great deal. The other sample soils are illustrative. Stabiliser rates and "no topsoil": Auroville Earth Institute; jar timings: Clemson Extension.

The shrinkage box

How to run it
  1. Grease a wooden or metal box, open on top, 30–40 mm square and 500–600 mm long.
  2. Wet the soil to a little past its liquid limit: a V-groove cut in it closes after about five taps on the box.
  3. Pack it in hard, corners first, and scrape the top level.
  4. Dry it seven days in the shade, or a day indoors and then in an oven at 110 °C.
  5. Push the bar to one end and measure the gap. Shrinkage is the gap over the wet length: FAO's example, 60 mm in a 600 mm box, is 10 %.

More than three large cracks besides the end gaps, and the soil is not suitable; more than 10 % shrinkage, and it is unfit for stabilising (FAO, Farm Structures).

Clay up close

Sizes from FAO: sand 2–0.06 mm, silt 0.06–0.002 mm, clay below 0.002 mm, so a sand grain can be a thousand times wider than a clay particle. Smectite clays such as montmorillonite can swell by up to 30 % in volume (Purdue Extension): water molecules push the mineral layers apart (NPTEL lecture notes), while kaolinite shows no shrink–swell to speak of (Burras, Iowa State). Black cotton soil is mostly montmorillonite (Katti 1978). The plates are drawn schematically.

Study

Eight ways to make a wall

The same 1 m panel, built eight ways and left half finished so you can see inside: the left half wears its plaster, the right half shows the raw build. Turn it round to see the back.

Two walls made by pressing earth

Rammed earth: damp soil poured about 100–150 mm deep and rammed, by hand or with a pneumatic rammer, to roughly half that depth (Studio Matrx 2026; Wikipedia gives 10–25 cm, compacted to about half) Medium; the forms can come off as soon as the wall is done (Wikipedia). Auroville rams its stabilised walls by hand in sliding formwork (Auroville Earth Institute). Block press: the Auram press 3000's 15-second cycle, 2.7–5.3 MPa and compression ratio of 1.77 for a 9 cm block, drawn as loose fill 1.77 times the block's height; about 850 blocks a day (Auroville Earth Institute).

Three more walls, step by step

Where the steps and numbers come from

Adobe: Hohn 2011, ABCs of Making Adobe Bricks (New Mexico State University guide G-521): soils with no more than 30 % clay (table 1), soak at least 12 hours, wet the forms, sand the drying ground, strike off, at least three days before handling, then on edge, three to four weeks before rough handling, loose stacks in showery weather; a common size of 4 × 10 × 14 in at 35–40 lb (table 2) Medium.

Blocks: the Auroville Earth Institute (no topsoil, about 5 % cement, 2–4 MPa, four weeks' curing and two of drying, a team of 11–13 for one press) and ITDG Zimbabwe, How to make stabilised soil blocks (a 5–6 mm sieve, dry mixing to one colour, the drop test from shoulder height, stacks no more than five high, damp 4–5 days under plastic, not used before 28 days) Medium.

Straw bale: the 2015 International Residential Code, appendix S (AS102.1, AS103.4–5, AS104, AS105.4.2, AS105.6.5–6, AS106.12.1), a US code: a guide where your own rules are silent High. The drawings are schematic. Awaiting builder review.

Study

The lime cycle

Lime plaster is limestone that has been taken apart and put back together on your wall. Select a stage.

Sources

The cycle, the 900 °C burn and slaking with heat: Lime.org.uk; the violent, steaming slake, carbonation from the air and lime's openness to vapour: ASBP Lime Group 2026; lime into water, putty kept wet while it matures: IS 1635:1992 (summary); kankar: FIBIS; hydraulic lime from clay-rich stone: the Building Conservation Directory; how fast a coat carbonates: the review by Despotou et al. 2016; cracks closing as lime dissolves and re-deposits: Lubelli, Nijland and van Hees 2011, who find it works only up to a point. The masses follow from the formulas, per mole CaCO₃ 100 g, CaO 56, CO₂ 44, H₂O 18 and Ca(OH)₂ 74, so 44 % of the stone's weight is carbon dioxide. Safety: see Tools and the lime safety fact sheet.

Subject

Plasters and binders

What holds natural walls and plasters together, how each binder sets, and what the traditional additives really do. Every number here is also in the shared material data table, with its source.

How each binder sets

Watch lime turn back into stone

Field test

The pink test

Spray a fresh break with phenolphthalein: lime that is still lime turns pink; carbonated lime stays clear.

How fast the front moves, and source

The front moves with the square root of time, about 1 mm per √day in typical lime mortar: 10 mm in about 100 days, 20 mm in about 400. A plaster a few centimetres thick finishes in one to two years; a deep wall joint can take decades. Source: Despotou et al. 2016. Phenolphthalein starts to colour at about pH 8.2.

From rammed and oiled earth to Kota stone and Chettinad tiles: how each floor is built up, how it feels under a bare foot, and which rooms it suits.

Seven floors

How does it feel underfoot?

Why stone feels cold

It is how fast the floor pulls heat

Same room, same temperature: stone draws heat out of a bare foot fast, timber slowly. That rate is set by the floor's effusivity, √(k ρ c). Cool stone is a gift in May and a chill in December.

Subject

Timber and bamboo

The wood in an earth house: why bamboo gets eaten, how to treat it, how culms are joined, and how strong it really is.

Inside a culm

Why bamboo gets eaten, and sources

Bamboo has no heartwood and almost none of the natural toxins that protect teak. Its inner tissue is packed with starch, and the powder-post beetle Dinoderus walks in through the cut ends to eat it. So the first defence is less starch: the right season, mature culms, and a week standing in shade.

Sources: Odisha Bamboo Development Agency (season, beetles, shade-curing) · Guadua Bamboo (age, flowering) · IS 9096 summary (puncturing diaphragms).

Make it last

Where will it live?
Soaking, step by step
  1. Fell, then shade-cure the culms upright for 7–10 days.
  2. Cut to length and puncture every diaphragm with a long steel rod, or drill each internode.
  3. Dissolve the boric acid and borax in water (warm water is faster) in a tank, pit or lined trench long enough for the culms.
  4. Sink the culms, weighted down; thicker walls need longer. ISO 22156 asks for about 4 kg of salts per m³ of bamboo indoors.
  5. Lift, drain on end, and dry slowly in shade to under 20 % moisture before building.

Ratio and strengths from Guadua Bamboo and the IS 9096 summary, which notes conflicting target moistures (25–30 % in IS 9096, ≤ 20 % in ISO). Awaiting builder review.

How strong is it?

Reading the bars, and sources

A culm varies with species, age, height in the plant and moisture, so its bar is solid to the low end and faded to the high end. Teak is one tested average at 12 % moisture; steel is the IS 2062 E250 minimum. No source we used gives teak in tension, so that bar is left empty rather than guessed. For design, use characteristic values from ISO 22156 or IS 15912 tests on your own bamboo.

Sources: InfraLens bamboo Medium · CIRAD Tropix teak · Tata Steel IS 2062.

Joining culms

Keeping wood alive

Choosing timber

Durability classes and confidence

IS 401 sorts timber by natural durability from graveyard tests (stakes in the ground): Class I lasts over 120 months, Class II 60–120, Class III under 60 (IS 401 summary). Rows marked Low are common Indian trade knowledge not yet matched to a published test; awaiting a source and builder review.

Subject

Finishes, paints and sealants

The last coat decides whether an earth wall can dry. Limewash, clay paint, casein, oils and waxes: what binds each one, how it sets, how open it stays to vapour, and how to mix it.

Six finishes

Can the wall still breathe?

What sd means, and sources

A finish's sd is the thickness of still air that would hold back water vapour as much as the finish does. EN ISO 7783 groups paints into four classes: under 0.14 m is highly breathable, over 1.5 m is low; heritage practice asks for under 0.05 m on solid walls. Grey points are published or makers' figures; clay-coloured points were measured in a lab to EN ISO 12572, and the two can disagree widely. In a 2024 study of Dublin walls, paint made little difference while the wall was moderately damp; near saturation, high-sd paints kept moisture in.

Sources: Walker et al. 2024 · Heritage Consulting · EN ISO 7783 classes · Keim · Earthborn. No measured sd was found for casein or linseed oil paint.

After a storm: how fast does the wall dry?

The drying model

Moisture leaves the wet layer by diffusion through two resistances in series, the wet earth (μ × 20 mm) and the finish (its sd); drying time is taken as proportional to their sum, with bare earth as 1. Earth μ measured on rammed earth: 16.6 by dry cup (Narloch et al. 2021) and 4 by wet cup (Stazi 2016, cited there). Relative times only; it ignores liquid flow, sun and wind. Illustrative Low.

How much limewash?

Additives

Plain lime and water lasted best

Which finish where?

Oily rags can catch fire on their own. Linseed oil gives off heat as it cures, and a crumpled rag holds that heat until it ignites. Lay rags flat outdoors to dry, or keep them under water in a closed metal tin, and never put them in a bin (British Coatings Federation).

Guidance drawn from the sources above; awaiting builder review.

Subject

Foundations and plinths

An earth wall needs "a good hat and good boots". The boots: what carries the wall, how water is kept from climbing into it, and what to do on black cotton soil.

Five foundations

Why water climbs: every pore is a tube

Rising damp at your foundation

Four ways to stop it

Sources and the physics

Rise heights are the ranges of Silin-Bekchurin (1958), via NPTEL; gravel is computed. The equivalent pore size is from Jurin's law, h = 2γ / (ρ g r), about 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ / r metres for water. The rising-damp figure shows rise in the soil only, not wicking through the plinth masonry.

Damp-proof courses: InfraLens on IS 3067. The NZ earth standard requires a DPC between foundation and earth wall, and a floor at least 150 mm above outside ground (BRANZ Bulletin 667); the Indian code minimum plinth is 150 mm, typical 450–600 mm (NBC via InfraLens). IS 13827 asks earthen buildings for a plinth at least 300 mm above ground and above flood level, and a footing at least 400 mm deep (cl. 10.3.2, 10.3.4; full text).

Black cotton soil moves every year

Building it

Four steps

  1. BoreAuger the stem to at least 3.5 m.
  2. Under-reamOpen the bulbs with an under-reaming tool, the top one at least 1.75 m down.
  3. CastLower the steel cage and concrete the pile.
  4. Grade beamSpan the pile heads, held at least 80 mm clear of the ground.
Sources

Numbers from IS 2911 (Part 3):1980; the safe-load row is read from a scanned table, so verify it. Swelling of 20–40 % and an active zone of about 2–3 m are given by the InfraLens handbook; IS 2911 asks for the top bulb at least 1.75 m down and a pile at least 3.5 m long, so the depth of the moving zone depends on the site. The figure draws it shallower than the bulbs. Design and load testing by an engineer.

How wide must the footing be?

How the width is worked out

Width = load per metre ÷ safe bearing capacity (kN/m²). Bearing values are IS 1904 presumptive figures via the InfraLens handbook, for preliminary design only; halve them for sand below the water table. Wall densities from the Walls section; the roof load is your estimate (a light tiled roof over a 5 m span is roughly 5 kN/m) Low. Not a substitute for a soil test.

Which foundation where?

Guidance drawn from the sources above; awaiting builder review. For the reference house, see Decision 02 in Why this, not that.

Subject

Openings, lintels and arches

Every door and window is a hole in a wall that wants to be solid. Where an earth wall can take openings, how wide, and how to carry the wall over them.

Where can the openings go?

Where these rules come from

From the text of IS 13827:1993 with Amendments 1 and 2, cl. 10.1.2 to 10.1.8: openings no wider than 1.2 m and at least 1.2 m from outside corners; their total no more than 50 % of the wall in zone II, 40 % in zones III and IV, 33⅓ % in zone V; lintels bearing 300 mm each side; height up to 8 t; length between cross-walls up to 10 t and 64 t²/h. The pier rule follows from the lintel bearing. An earlier draft used a secondary summary (¼ of the height and 600 mm to a corner); the standard is stricter.

What a lintel really carries

How an arch stands

The safe theorem, and the model behind the figure

Bricks and earth blocks have almost no strength in tension. An arch stands because the load finds a path of pure compression through it, the line of thrust. If any such line fits inside the ring, the arch can stand (the safe theorem); if it stays in the middle third, every joint stays closed. Where the line touches a face, the joint opens like a hinge; four hinges make a mechanism and it folds.

The figure loads the arch evenly across the span (its own weight at 18 kN/m³ plus the wall above), adds the point load if you set one, and searches for the thrust line that best fits the ring: the bending-moment diagram of a simple beam with the same loads, divided by the horizontal thrust H. It passes through the centre of each springing, which is slightly conservative. Thickness rules: Auroville Earth Institute (semicircular t = S/5, or S/10 with loaded haunches) and Boothby 2021 (S/t ≤ 40 r/S). Teaching model; awaiting builder review.

How arches and vaults are built

Centring: Wikipedia. The Nubian vault: the Auroville Earth Institute, La Voûte Nubienne: walls about 60 cm, a gable about 40 cm leaned in about 1.5 cm a metre, a guide cable with a ring and a cord, rings tilted about 60°, bricks 24 × 12 × 4.5 cm, an inside width of no more than about 3.2 m, side walls raised 8–10 courses and filled with earth, then a mud coat, a plastic sheet and a render about 5 cm thick (the page also says at least 6 cm) Medium. Drawn schematically; awaiting builder review.

Subject

Structure and earthquakes

Earth walls are heavy and weak in tension. Pick your zone, shake two walls, and watch the five ways earth houses fail, each with its fix.

Your seismic zone

Z is the peak ground acceleration the code plans for, as a fraction of gravity. A revised code with a new Zone VI was withdrawn in March 2026, so the 2016 zones apply.

Shake two walls

How the model works, and what it leaves out

Each wall is a rigid block of earth with no tensile strength. The free wall rocks on its base corners (Housner's rocking equation, losing energy at each impact by the standard restitution); it starts to rock when ground acceleration exceeds g × t/h, and falls once it tips past its diagonal. The tied wall is held at the top, so it can only fail by folding at mid-height: by virtual work, the inertia W·a·h/4 must exceed the work against gravity W·t, so it needs 4 t/h × g, four times as much.

Left out: roof weight on the wall (it helps a tied wall and hurts a free one), cracking and damage, corners letting go, and the stronger shaking higher up a building. The record is synthetic, not a real earthquake. This is a teaching model, not a design check.

Sources: Lestuzzi 2023 (threshold t/h) · rocking of rigid blocks, arXiv 2106.11741 (Housner's equation, restitution) · zone factors, IS 1893 via InfraLens · withdrawal of IS 1893:2025. The 4 t/h result is derived here, not quoted.

Five ways an earth house fails

What your zone asks for

Sources and caveats

Rules for earthen walls from the text of IS 13827:1993 with Amendments 1 (1995) and 2 (2002). The original applied to zones III–V; the amendments added the zone II limits (50 % openings, one band). The copy is a scan read by OCR: the zone V share prints as “33)” and is read as 33⅓ %. The standard itself warns that earthen buildings are weak against water and earthquakes and should preferably be avoided in flood-prone, high-rainfall areas and zones IV and V.

Zones are those of IS 1893 (Part 1): 2016. A 2025 revision added a Zone VI for the Himalayan belt and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands; it was withdrawn in March 2026 and the 2016 zones apply again (ETV Bharat, March 2026). Check for a new revision before you build.

Study

Sun and shade

The reference house at 17.4° N, on the Deccan. Move the month and the hour, stretch the eaves, turn the house, and watch which walls the sun reaches. Earth walls store whatever heat lands on them.

Share of each wall in direct sun

At this latitude the sun passes north of overhead from early May to early August, so the north wall gets early and late sun too. East and west walls catch the most sun, about 690 W/m² at 8 am and 4 pm on a clear summer day in Hyderabad, and the west wall gets it with the hottest air: the reference house keeps its west wall blank.

How much sun each wall takes, as India's energy code weighs it

With these eaves, the windows get this share of the sun they would get with none (Eco-Niwas Samhita's shading factors for overhangs).

How the sun is worked out

Solar declination by Cooper's equation, δ = 23.45° sin(360° (284 + n)/365), with the standard altitude and azimuth formulas (pvlib, after Duffie and Beckman), in solar time, for the 15th of each month. Checked against NOAA's solar position equations: on those days Cooper stays within 1.4° of NOAA, furthest in October. The Astronomical Society of India gives Hyderabad's zero-shadow days, when the noon sun is straight overhead, as 9 May and 3 August; the dates worked out here land within a day of them. The latitude follows the place chosen in Ways in. Shading counts the eaves only: trees, neighbours and hills are ignored.

Sun on the walls: SP 41's hour-by-hour table for Hyderabad (SP 41:1987, Table 5). It names no date, but its south wall gets no direct sun at all, which puts it between early May and early August; it peaks at 686 W/m² on the east wall at 8:00 and on the west wall at 16:00, and at 221 on the north wall Medium, read from a scan. The bars for the four walls use the orientation factor of Eco-Niwas Samhita 2018 (Table 9), a weighting of the direct and diffuse sun on a wall by the way it faces; its eight factors average 1.0. The eave figures use the same code's projection factor (Annexure 7: the eave's depth divided by the height from the window sill to the eave's lowest edge) and its shading factors for overhangs (Tables 10 and 11), here for the 1.1 m windows with sills 0.9 m up. Eaves of 400–700 mm are quoted for keeping rain off cob walls in England (New Forest National Park); in the Indian sun they shade as well.

Study

Thermal mass: the wall as a clock

A thick earth wall slows the day's heat on its way in and lets only a little of it through. Choose a climate and a wall, play the day, and watch the heat travel through the wall and arrive in the room hours later.

How the wall model works, and where its numbers come from

Simulated one-dimensional heat flow through a single layer, run until the days repeat. The outside air swings on a smooth daily curve from the normal low at 3:00 to the normal high at 15:00 Low: 1991–2020 normals for Hyderabad (Begumpet) from Climate-Zone, and for Mumbai (Colaba) from Wikipedia, after the Tokyo Climate Center. A wall facing the sun gets SP 41's hour-by-hour sun for Hyderabad (SP 41:1987, Table 5, a clear day between May and August), cut for cloud in the monsoon (×0.4), for the winter sun (×0.85) and for coastal haze (×0.9) Low. The face absorbs 65 % of it, a mid-to-dark earth colour (IES lists absorptivity by material; Midland Brick puts red brick near 0.75, and anything over 0.6 in the dark class) Low. Surface resistances are 0.04 outside and 0.13 inside, from Eco-Niwas Samhita Table 6. The room air is held at the daily mean. Real rooms also depend on the roof, windows, ventilation and people, so read the numbers as a comparison, not a forecast.

Materials: fired brick, CSEB and concrete block from Eco-Niwas Samhita 2018, Table 7 (the concrete-block row prints a specific heat of 200, which cannot be right; dense concrete's 880 is used). Earth conductivity by density after Minke, and adobe at 0.81, from Cuitiño-Rosales et al. 2020: cob at 1,700 kg/m³ is taken between Minke's 0.80 and 0.95. Specific heat of earth 850 J/kg·K, from stabilised rammed earth (Hall and Allinson, 830–870) and mud phuska (880). Straw bale 0.052 W/m·K (Passive House Institute) with straw board's specific heat. Every value is also in the material data table.

Study

Building physics

Heat, water vapour, humidity and air: what moves through an earth wall and a room, and why the natural materials behave so differently. Drag the round handles.

Heat and vapour through a wall

How the wall is worked out, and the values

Heat: the layers add up as resistances, R = Rsi + Σ d/λ + Rse, with U = 1/R and the surface resistances of the Indian residential code (0.13 and 0.04 m²K/W). Vapour: the Glaser method of EN ISO 13788. Each layer resists vapour like a thickness of still air, sd = μ·d; the vapour line runs straight from inside to outside in sd and may not rise above saturation; where it is forced down onto the saturation line, water condenses at the rate set by the change of slope.

Values: earth λ 0.95 (Cuitiño-Rosales 2020) with μ 16.6 (Narloch 2021, dry cup); CSEB λ 1.20 (Eco-Niwas Samhita) with μ 24 (6 % cement, Narloch); lime plaster λ 0.7, μ 7 (WUFI data); clay-straw plaster λ 0.34, μ 11 (Liuzzi 2016); straw bale λ 0.052 (Passive House Institute) with μ 1.5 assumed Low; acrylic paint sd 0.53 m (Walker 2024, measured); plastic sheet sd 6.6 m (WUFI generic retarder). Steady state only: it ignores the wall's moisture storage, rain and sun, which matter a great deal for earth. Use it to see the direction of risk, not to certify a wall.

How warm is comfortable?

Adaptive comfort

Comfort moves with the season

In a house with open windows, people accept a warmer room in a hot month. The India Model for Adaptive Comfort, from surveys across Indian climates, puts the most comfortable temperature at 0.54 × the month's mean outdoor temperature + 12.83 °C. Drag the line to an indoor temperature: green months suit 90 % of people, amber 80 %.

Black dots: Hyderabad monthly mean (1991–2020, Begumpet). Model: Manu et al. 2016, valid for monthly means of 12.5–31 °C; May (hatched) is hotter than that, so its band is held at the 31 °C value.

Walls that breathe humidity

What the moisture buffer value means, and sources

The moisture buffer value (MBV) is the water a surface takes up per m² for each 1 % rise in humidity, measured over 8 hours at 75 % and 16 at 33 % (the NORDTEST method). Litres = MBV × area × 42 % ÷ 1000. Classes: under 0.5 limited, 0.5–1 moderate, 1–2 good, above 2 excellent (Rode et al. 2005). Clay plaster 1.56–1.89 and with paper 2.34–2.73 (Nutt 2020); gypsum, cellular concrete and hemp (Khaled 2023); spruce, brick, concrete (Rode 2005). Finishes cut buffering: linseed oil 39–50 %, beeswax 29 %, limewash 7–13 % (Santos et al. 2024, see Plasters and binders). When temperature and humidity swing together, a clay base coat buffered only 0.34–0.57 (Cascione 2019): treat the litres as a lab comparison, not a room forecast.

Air that moves itself

Stack effect

Height pulls air

Warm air inside is lighter than the cooler air outside. Give it a way out high and a way in low and the house ventilates itself, with no wind and no fan. The flow grows with the square root of the height between the openings and of the temperature difference: four times the height gives twice the air.

Q = C·A·√(2 g h ΔT / T), with C = 0.65 (stack effect), two equal openings in series (A/√2), room air at 30 °C, wind ignored. Room of 48 m³.

Subject

Water and sanitation

Three waters pass through every house: rain off the roof, used water from the kitchen and bath, and the toilet. Keep them apart: catch the rain clean, clean the greywater in a planted bed, and keep the toilet pits far from the well. Set the household once: every figure below follows it.

Household
tap a person; every figure follows

Follow the water

Three waters

Keep them apart

  • Rain off the roof: clean enough to store once the first, dirty flush is thrown away. What the tank cannot hold goes back into the ground.
  • Greywater from the kitchen, bath and laundry: soap, grease and food, cleaned in a planted bed and given to the garden.
  • Toilet waste: into pits that hold the solids and let the liquid soak away, far from any well.

Watch the film, or tap a step. Each step links to its own figure below.

Roof to tank

Roof water

Keep the tank clean from the roof down

What spoils a tank comes off a dusty roof with the first rain, or gets in through an open lid. A leaf screen, a first flush, a closed, dark tank and a floating intake keep it out; a recharge pit takes what the tank cannot hold.

From the Texas Manual on Rainwater Harvesting (2005), pp. 8–18, and the Central Ground Water Board's Simple and practical methods of artificial recharge (2025), pp. 7–14, 37. The first-flush volume follows the roof area set in the next figure.

How big a tank?

How the tank is worked out, and sources

A day-by-day water balance. Each day the roof adds its plan area × that month's rain, spread evenly over the month's days, × a runoff coefficient: 0.85 for clay tiles and 0.8 for metal, inside the ranges of the KUIDFC trainers' manual (0.8–0.9 and 0.7–0.9). The household then draws its water; whatever does not fit in the tank overflows. Three years are run so each year starts as the last one ended. "Never runs dry" is the largest running shortfall over the year (the sequent-peak method), rounded up to 0.5 kL. The tank is drawn as a round tank 2 m tall, beside a person 1.7 m tall.

Rain: Begumpet monthly normals, 1991–2020, about 828 mm a year (Climate-Zone, from 23 years of records) Medium. An average year only: dry years come, so leave a margin. For scale, rural India plans at least 55 litres a person a day for everything (Jal Jeevan Mission guidelines, para 6.1, as quoted by the CAG). First flush, screens, covers and the floating intake: Texas Manual on Rainwater Harvesting (2005), pp. 8–18. A 150 mm pipe holds about 17.7 litres a metre. Recharge pit: an inverted filter of pebbles, gravel and sand on top, about 2 × 1 × 1 m for a 100 m² roof, its top sand scraped off before every monsoon, only where the water table stays deeper than 3 m after the monsoon and away from septic tanks and soak pits (CGWB 2025) Medium.

How a twin-pit toilet works

Twin pits

One pit fills while the other rests

A pour-flush pan needs only a mug of water. Behind it, two pits sit side by side: one is used until it is full, then the flow is switched to the other. By the time the second is full, the first has rested about two years and its contents can be dug out by hand and used as a soil conditioner.

Pan and water seal: Eawag Compendium, pour flush toilet. Pits 1 m apart, more than 1 m from foundations, lined to their full depth with the top 30 cm mortared, one at a time, about two years' rest, dug out rather than pumped: Eawag Compendium, twin pits. How much each pit holds: IS 12314 and the WEDC guide, below.

Where the toilet goes

Three sources that disagree, and why the plan shows two circles

The Indian standard is the most lenient. IS 12314:1987, cl. 9: 3 m from a well or tube well in fine soil (effective size 0.2 mm or less) where the pit bottom stays 2 m above the highest groundwater, 10 m where groundwater comes closer; in coarser soil the same distances, but only with a sealed bottom and a 500 mm envelope of fine sand. Pits at least their own effective depth apart (cl. 4.4), at least two years' storage (cl. 4.1.4), solids 0.04 m³ a person a year in a dry pit and 0.095 in a wet pit emptied every two years (table 1). Read from a scanned copy Medium: check the printed standard.

The WEDC guide sets distance by ground (Reed 2014, table 2): silt 10 m, fine silty sand 15, weathered basement not fractured 25, medium sand 50, gravel 500; in fractured rock no horizontal distance protects a water source. Sludge (table 3): 40 litres a person a year in water and 60 dry, with degradable cleansing, plus 50 % for the shallow pits of twin-pit toilets. The Eawag Compendium (Tilley et al. 2014): pits 1 m apart, more than 1 m from foundations, normally at least 30 m from a water source, and about two years' rest before emptying. Sludge here: 0.04 (IS 12314, dry) to 0.06 m³ (WEDC, twin pit) a person a year; a pit 1 m across holds about 0.8 m³ for each metre of depth. The shaded circle is the WEDC distance for the ground you pick, drawn round the pits; the inner circle is the Indian minimum. The plan has one well: count the neighbours' wells and bore wells too.

Greywater into a garden

Horizontal-flow bed

Roots and stones do the work

Water from the kitchen, bath and laundry carries soap, grease and food. Settled first, it creeps sideways through a lined bed of gravel planted with reeds, below the surface, and bacteria living on the stones and roots clean it on the way. Not for raw toilet water.

Sizes from the Eawag Compendium (Tilley et al. 2014): about 5–10 m² for each person, gravel 3–32 mm, 0.5–1 m deep, water held 5–15 cm below the top. It needs a lot of land and removes little of the nutrients.

Guidance drawn from the sources above; awaiting builder review. Local rules may ask for more.

Subject

Kitchen and hearth

The one room where fire, water and the earth wall meet. Get the smoke out first, give the fire a stove that burns it clean, and keep the wall by the sink dry.

Get the smoke out

Smoke

The fuel matters more than the room

About 2.1 billion people still cook on open fires or inefficient stoves. The smoke killed an estimated 2.9 million people in 2021, and it falls hardest on the women and children who spend longest by the hearth (WHO).

  1. A clean fuel. WHO counts solar, electricity, biogas, LPG, natural gas and alcohol fuels as clean where you cook.
  2. A wood stove that meets WHO’s targets, with its own chimney. The rocket stove below shows how such stoves are built.
  3. A smoke hood and flue over the old hearth: about 75 % less smoke in two Kenyan villages.
  4. Bigger eaves gaps: about 60 % less where the smoke was worst, but no bigger than you need.
  5. A window: light and air, but it took out less smoke than expected.

Watch the film, or tap a step.

Sources

People, deaths and clean fuels: WHO fact sheet (December 2025). Stove targets, 0.80 mg/min of fine particles and 0.59 g/min of carbon monoxide with a chimney or hood, 0.23 mg/min and 0.16 g/min without: WHO, 2014. Hoods, eaves and windows in Kajiado and West Kenya, 50 households: Bates, Bruce, Doig and Gitonga, Boiling Point 48 (ITDG, 2002). The article gives the means but not the period they were taken over. 82 % less smoke and 30 % less firewood: Practical Action. Gas: PMUY safety tips.

A stove that burns clean

Rocket stove

Burn the wood, not the smoke

Smoke is fuel that has not burned. Larry Winiarski’s rocket stove burns it with three ideas: a short chimney straight above the fire, light insulation round it so it runs hot, and a tube the same size all the way through, so the air never chokes.

The numbers under the film are the bar a portable biomass chulha has to clear in India. IS 13152 (Part 1): 2013 asks for at least 25 % thermal efficiency with natural draught and 35 % with a fan. It caps carbon monoxide at 5 g, and particles at 350 mg (150 mg with a fan), for every megajoule that reaches the pot.

A home-built stove has not been tested against either. Use it under a hood, or outdoors, until it has. Sources: Winiarski’s principles (Aprovecho, 2002); BIS consumer guide.

An earth oven

Earth oven

The door keeps the heat in

Kiko Denzer’s earth oven is a dome of sand and clay over a brick floor. Heap damp sand into a form, pack mud over it a hand’s width thick, cut the door, and dig the sand out once the mud is leather-hard. When it is dry, fire it for two or three hours, until the soot burns off the inside of the dome.

The rule that matters is the door: 63 % of the dome’s inside height. Hot air rises and stays in the dome above it, while smoke spills out over the top of the door.

  • Floor: 51–69 cm (20–27 in) across: red or fire bricks on 10–15 cm of tamped sand.
  • Mud: one part clay subsoil to one to three parts sharp sand. A packed ball dropped from chest height should hold together.
  • Base: at waist height if you will use it often.
How the oven is sized

Everything except the litres of mud comes from Kiko Denzer’s article in Mother Earth News: a 20–27 inch floor; a sand form a few inches higher than half the floor, 16–20 inches for a 27 inch floor; a door 63 % of the dome’s inside height, and a third to a half of the floor wide; a first layer 3–4 inches thick. The figure draws the dome as half an ellipsoid. The litres are our arithmetic for a shell 7.5–10 cm thick on that shape, with nothing taken off for the door Low. Denzer adds more layers and a finish plaster if you want them; this figure shows only the first.

Plan the room

  • Size: at least 5.0 m² and 2.4 m high, with windows and vents of at least a tenth of the floor area (NBC 2016 Part 3, as summarised by InfraLens). Your state’s bye-laws can ask for more.
  • The sink: stone or tile behind it and the platform, or lime and tadelakt. Anything the water reaches must be impervious (BRANZ), and earth has to be kept dry (Level). The waste runs through a trap to a grease trap and the planted bed (Water and sanitation).
  • The fire: under a hood, or in a stove with its own chimney, with a window near it for light. Fire safety, above all under thatch, is not covered yet (Coverage).
  • Gas: the cylinder upright on the floor, never in a pit or a closed cupboard, and the stove on a platform above it. A Suraksha hose, replaced before its five years are up (PMUY).

Guidance drawn from the sources above; awaiting builder review.

Subject

Bathroom

The wettest room in an earth house. Slope the floor to a trap, line every wall the water reaches, and let the room dry out between baths.

Slope the floor, line the splashes

Wet room

Water goes where the floor sends it

An Indian bathroom is usually wet all over: a bucket, a tap and a drain in the floor. So the whole floor has to fall to the trap, and every wall the water reaches needs a lining it cannot soak into.

  • Wet zone: 1.5 m round the tap or shower. Line its walls at least 1.8 m up, and 300 mm above a shower head (BRANZ).
  • Earth wall: earth plaster above the lining and outside the wet zone, where the air can dry it.
  • Fall: 1 in 50 to 1 in 80 towards the drain. BRANZ and the Australian code disagree on the exact figure: tap a fall to compare.

Drag the trap and the tap. The corners show how much higher the floor must be than the drain.

Where the numbers come from

Falls: BRANZ asks for at least 1 in 60 in an enclosed shower and 1 in 50 in a level-access one, over 1.5 m from the shower. The 2016 Australian code (South Australia) asks for 1 in 60 to 1 in 80 in the shower and 1 in 80 to 1 in 100 in the rest of the room. Linings: impervious to at least 1.8 m and 300 mm above the shower head, and a membrane over the whole floor turned 150 mm up the walls (BRANZ; the membrane is a recommendation). Trap: a water seal of at least 50 mm (EN 1253-1). Room sizes: NBC 2016 Part 3, via InfraLens. Two assumptions are ours Low: a bucket bath is treated like an open shower, wet for 1.5 m round the tap, and the shower head is taken at 2 m. These are New Zealand and Australian rules: a guide where Indian rules are silent, not Indian law.

Hot water from the roof

Solar water heater

The sun heats the bath water

Water warms in a dark panel facing south and rises into a tank above it, while colder water sinks back down to the panel. A heater of 100 litres a day is enough for a family of four or five, needs about 3 m² of roof and can save up to 1,500 units of electricity a year (TERI, for MNRE). It heats water to 60–80 °C (HAREDA).

Sized at 25 litres a person a day, an NBC norm as summarised by InfraLens Low. Flat-plate collectors are made to IS 12933 (HAREDA).

The rest of the room

  • Size: at least 1.8 m² for a bathroom and 1.1 m² for a separate WC, 2.4 m high, with windows and vents of at least a tenth of the floor area (NBC 2016 Part 3, via InfraLens).
  • Let it dry: a vent high in the wall, so the room dries out between baths. Earth must be kept from moisture (Level).
  • Under the floor: a membrane across the whole floor, turned at least 150 mm up every wall (BRANZ recommends it).
  • Pipes: through the earth walls in sleeves, set before the plaster (stage 11 of Build it).
  • Or keep the earth out: build the wet walls of stone or fired brick, and keep the earth for the dry rooms. This one is our suggestion Low
  • The toilet: a pour-flush pan on twin pits, and the bath water to the planted bed (Water and sanitation).

Guidance drawn from the sources above; awaiting builder review. Local rules may ask for more.

Subject

Plumbing

Clean water in under pressure, used water out downhill, and none of it inside an earth wall. Height gives the pressure, the fall keeps the drains clear, and a trap and a vent keep the smell out.

Water through the house

Supply and drains

Two systems that never meet

  • Supply: pumped up once, to a tank, then down to every tap by gravity. Pressure comes from height alone.
  • Drains: from a trap at every outlet, downhill all the way to the pits and the planted bed, past a chamber at every bend.
  • Vent: a pipe from the drains to above the roof, so the traps keep their water.

Earth walls and water do not mix: keep the pipes where a leak shows, and sleeve the ones that must pass through a wall.

Watch the film, or tap a step.

How high should the tank be?

Gravity supply

A metre of height, a tenth of a bar

Water pushes down with its own weight: every metre between the water in the tank and a tap adds about 0.1 bar. A shower wants about 5 m of that, 8 m to be good; an instant geyser or a mixer needs 0.3–0.5 bar just to start (Studio Matrx).

How much to store: IS 1172 plans 70–100 litres a person a day for a house without a full flushing system and 150–200 in towns with one, or 135 for small houses; Studio Matrx plans 135 for homes with full plumbing. The figure sizes a day’s store at 135 litres for the people in Your house.

  • Pipes: 32–40 mm out of the tank, 25 mm along the house, 15–20 mm to each fitting, and 20 mm for a shower on a low tank (Studio Matrx, indicative).
  • Short of height? Raise the tank on a tower, or put a pressure pump on the shower line.

Figures from Studio Matrx are indicative, not a code Low. The figure ignores what pipes and bends take, so read it as the most you can get.

Drains that fall

Building drainage

Downhill all the way

A drain has to fall steadily enough to carry the solids with the water: a self-cleansing speed of about 0.75 m/s when half full. IS 1742 asks for at least 1 in 57 for a 100 mm pipe and 1 in 100 for a 150 mm one; builders often lay them at 1 in 40 and 1 in 60 (Studio Matrx, after IS 1742; external drains).

Over a long run the fall adds up, and the last chamber ends up deep. Drag the end of the run to see how deep.

  • Chambers: at every junction, bend and change of slope or pipe size, and about every 30 m on a straight run, so every length can be rodded.
  • Their size: 450 × 450 to 600 × 600 mm inside up to about 0.9 m deep; 600 × 600 to 900 × 600 mm to 1.5 m; a manhole beyond that.
  • Outside the kitchen and bath: a gully trap takes their water into the drain (IS 1742).

Rules for the pipes

  • Keep water out of the earth: run pipes along internal walls, on the face of a wall or in the floor, where a leak shows. Where one has to cross an earth wall, sleeve it the full width, with no joint inside (Straw Works, writing about straw walls; the same holds for earth).
  • A trap at every outlet: at least 50 mm of water in a WC or a floor trap, 40 mm in other fittings (IS 5329, via Studio Matrx).
  • A vent above the roof: its top at least 150 mm above a roof, 2.1 m above a terrace and 0.9 m above an opening window, and at least 32 mm across (UIPC-I 2017, from the Indian Plumbing Association).
  • Keep the three waters apart: rain to the tank, kitchen and bath water to the planted bed, the toilet to the pits, and the well clear of them all (Water and sanitation).

Indian standards are cited through published summaries, not the standards themselves; awaiting builder review. Local bye-laws can ask for more.

Subject

Wiring, earthing and solar

Every cable in a conduit, a breaker that trips before a person is hurt, two good earths, and panels on the south side of the roof. Plan it all before the walls go up.

From the meter to the socket

The board

A breaker for people, a breaker for each circuit

The board holds a main switch, an RCCB that cuts the supply when current leaks to earth, and a miniature circuit breaker for each circuit, matched to its wire.

  • Wire: CPWD asks for at least 1.5 mm² of copper for lights and 4 mm² for power (CPWD, cl. 3.12). Sockets for small appliances commonly take 2.5 mm², a geyser or an air conditioner 4–6 mm² (Studio Matrx, indicative).
  • RCCB: 30 mA to protect people. British rules require one on every socket circuit (BS 7671, 411.3.3); CPWD puts one beside the incoming breaker of a residential quarter’s board (cl. 3.20); Tamil Nadu made them compulsory on new connections in 2021 (TNERC). India’s 2010 safety rules asked for one on loads above 5 kW (CEA, as summarised by Wikipedia).
  • Earth: two separate earth connections, in two or more pits (CEA). A plate of at least 60 × 60 cm, or a 40 mm GI pipe in a treated pit; rods spaced about their driven depth apart. Salt lowers the resistance but brings corrosion, and coke breeze is not recommended (IS 3043:1987).
  • Sockets: three-pin, with the earth pin wired; two-pin sockets are not allowed in CPWD work.

Watch the film, or tap a step.

Solar on your roof

Rooftop solar

Ten square metres a kilowatt

A kilowatt of panels needs about 10 m² of roof with no shade, and makes 4–5.5 units on a clear day (MNRE). Modules are warranted to give 90 % after 12 years and 80 % after 25, and need cleaning now and then.

With net metering, a two-way meter sends what you do not use to the grid and you pay only for the difference. Under PM Surya Ghar, households get ₹30,000 a kW for the first 2 kW and ₹18,000 for the third, at most ₹78,000 (scheme rates); 0–150 units a month suits 1–2 kW, 150–300 units 2–3 kW (scheme table).

Face the panels south. For the most direct sun in a year, tilt them at about your latitude; most large fixed systems in the US sit at 20–30° (EIA). On a sloping roof they take the roof’s pitch.

Rules for the wiring

  • Plan first: every switch, socket, light and the board, before the walls go up (Level).
  • In an earth wall: cables in PVC conduit to flush boxes made for masonry, with wooden blocks set in for fittings to hold (Level). Rigid PVC conduit to IS 9537 Part 3, cables to IS 694 (Studio Matrx). Cut the chases and fix the conduit before the plaster (stage 11 of Build it).
  • Who does it: an authorised electrical contractor, under the supervision of someone who holds a certificate of competency (CEA Regulations 2023, as summarised by K&S Partners).
  • Under thatch: wiring and panels near thatch are a fire risk. Fire safety is not covered yet (Coverage).

Indian rules are cited through summaries where the text was not to hand; awaiting review by a builder and a licensed electrician.

Subject

Repair and maintenance

An earth wall lasts as long as it is kept dry and looked after. Read the damage, plan the year around the monsoon, and patch a hollow the way conservators do.

Read the damage

A year of upkeep

Patch a hollow, step by step

    Where this comes from

    Most published repair guidance is for cob in Britain. The defects, hollows and major repairs follow the IHBC guidance note on earth walling (defects, surface hollows, stitching and major repairs); renders, shrinkage cracks, layering and paring follow Bouwens 1997; paring back and recent movement, Mike Wye. Limewash: Lime.org.uk. Termites: the Queensland building regulator, after AS 3660. Lintels and bands: IS 13827 (see Openings, and Structure and earthquakes). The year is set to Hyderabad's rain; move the jobs with your own monsoon.

    Guidance drawn from the sources above, mostly written for cob in Britain; awaiting builder review for Indian earth walls.

    Subject

    Tools

    The kit for an earth house is mostly hands, feet and simple iron. Pick a technique to see what it needs, and tap a tool for what it does.

    Lime burnsQuicklime and hydrated lime are caustic to eyes and skin. Wear goggles, gloves and clothes that cover arms and legs; add a dust mask with dry powder. Lime in an eye: flush it with plenty of water and get medical help at once. On skin: brush dry lime off, then wash with lots of water. Quicklime gets very hot when it meets water, hot enough to set things alight: slake it well away from anything that burns.Source: lime safety precautions fact sheet
    Sources

    Auram press figures from the Auroville Earth Institute (specifications, handling, equipment). Block and rammer sizes from IS 13827 (see Structure). Digging rates from CPWD output norms, via the InfraLens handbook. Lime care from Lime.org.uk and the IHBC (see Repair and maintenance). Local names are the common Hindi ones; they vary by region.

    Awaiting builder review.

    Subject

    Costing

    What the shell of your house takes in earth, stone, lime and working days, priced at Telangana's schedule of rates or at your own. It follows Your house; drag the plan here to try other sizes, and drag your crew's pace.

    Size the house

    Where the days go

    Your prices

    What is counted, what is not, and where the numbers come from

    The shell only: a rubble trench 600 mm deep and as wide as the wall plus 150 mm (IS 13827 asks for at least 400 mm deep; see Foundations for the width your soil needs), a stone plinth 450 mm high, walls 2.6 m high, a cross wall between each pair of rooms, one outside door, a door in each cross wall, two windows of 0.9 × 1.2 m to a room, lime plaster outside and earth plaster inside. Not counted: roof, floor, doors and windows, services, transport, scaffolding, the builder's margin and GST.

    Prices: Telangana Common Schedule of Rates 2022-23: mason class I ₹580 and mazdoor ₹520 a day; cement ₹5,600 a tonne; screened sand ₹830 and rough granite stone ₹263 a m³, at the quarry; earth from private land ₹72 a m³. The 2024-25 schedule is out and will be higher. Lime and straw are not in the schedule: put in a local quote. Prices you type stay in this browser only.

    Pace: CPWD output norms via the InfraLens handbook: digging murram 1.5–2 m³ a labourer a day; rubble masonry and brickwork 1–1.5 m³ a day for a mason and two helpers; two-coat plaster 6–8 m² and one-coat 10–12 m² a day. Block pressing: the Auram 3000, about 850 blocks a day with seven people (Auroville). We found no published pace for cob, rammed earth or adobe that we could check, so the walls bar starts at the brickwork pace Low: drag it to your crew's real pace. Filling the trench is taken at the digging pace, and moulding adobe at 150 blocks a person a day; both are assumptions Low.

    Quantities: wall densities from the Walls section (cob 1,700, adobe 1,600, rammed earth 2,050, CSEB 1,900 kg/m³); straw about 1.5 % of the cob by mass (Kabore and Ouellet-Plamondon 2024, citing a load test); 5 % cement in the blocks, as Auroville uses in its rammed earth (Auroville); lime plaster 1 : 3, taking the mortar as the volume of its sand; limewash at 4.5 m² a litre a coat (Mike Wye: 3–6); joints 10 mm for adobe and 5 mm for CSEB. For rammed earth, ERDEN's handbook puts it plainly: the raw material costs very little and labour is most of the cost (Rammed Earth Planning Handbook).

    An estimating aid, not a quotation; awaiting builder review.

    Decisions

    Why this, not that

    Every earth house is a chain of choices, each right for some soil, climate, budget or crew. The reference house: two rooms, one storey, red loam over murram on the Deccan plateau, about 800 mm of monsoon rain and summer days past 42 °C.

    Reference

    Material data

    One table for the numbers in this reference, each with its test or basis and its source. High: read from a standard or published measurements. Medium: a manufacturer's sheet, a secondary summary, or a reference value. Values from common practice are marked where they appear and are not listed here until sourced.

    Reference

    Library

    Every source this book draws on, in one place: what kind of source it is, which sections use it, and how many values in the material data table rest on it. Pages opened while researching but left out are here too, each with the reason.

    The cited list is read from the book itself: the material data table, the notes under each figure, the built forms and every section's links, so it grows with the book. The opened-but-not-cited list starts with the second batch of built forms; earlier rounds of research kept no such log.

    The words the craft uses, from the ground up.

    What this book covers, how well each part is sourced, and what is still missing. The page counts itself: the figures, data rows and links below are read from the book as it stands.
